children.note: Frontier models are the most capable general-purpose AI systems of the moment, mostly large language models that can now also see, hear, reason step by step and act as agents. This map covers who builds them, what they can do as of 2026, how they are measured, and what they cost in compute and energy.

How agents learn by trial and error from rewards: the core loop, policies and values, exploration, Q-learning, policy gradients, AlphaGo and AlphaZero, and the role of RL in training today's language models.

Alignment research tries to make AI systems pursue the goals their designers and users actually intend, and safety research checks whether they do. This map moves from the core problem to today's training methods, tools for looking inside models, testing, and the questions still open in 2026.

AI is now a working tool in research: it predicts protein shapes, forecasts weather, proposes new materials and drugs, and helps with maths. This map covers the landmark results, how they work, what they have not yet achieved, and early evidence from health research in Africa.

This map covers who builds them, what they can do as of 2026, how they are measured, and what they cost in compute and energy.

children.note: A moving label for the strongest general-purpose models of the day. Today's frontier becomes tomorrow's baseline, often within a year or two.
Large models trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks. LLMs are the best-known kind; image, audio and video models are others.

manas.q: What is a foundation model?

children.note: Decoder-only transformers are pre-trained to predict the next token, then fine-tuned to follow instructions. ChatGPT (late 2022) made this mass-market; GPT-4 (2023) was an early multimodal frontier model.
Labs training the largest models include OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta and xAI in the US, and DeepSeek, Alibaba (Qwen) and Moonshot AI in China, among others.
GPT (OpenAI), Gemini (Google DeepMind, announced Dec 2023), Claude (Anthropic, first released Mar 2023), Llama (Meta, from Feb 2023), Qwen (Alibaba) and DeepSeek. Names are examples, not rankings.
Training the biggest models costs hundreds of millions of US dollars in hardware, energy, data and staff. Adapting or using an existing model is far cheaper.

manas.q: Why do so few organisations train frontier models?

children.note: Closed models are used only through an app or API. Open-weight models publish their trained parameters so anyone can download, run and fine-tune them.
Many "open" models release weights but not training data or full code, and licences may restrict use. Read the licence before building on one.

manas.q: What is the difference between open-weight and fully open-source?

children.note: Meta's Llama began in Feb 2023 with research-only access; later versions allowed some commercial use. Llama 4 came out in April 2025.
A 671-billion-parameter open-weight reasoning model from China that performed comparably to OpenAI o1 at a much lower price per token. It showed the open/closed gap can be small.

manas.q: Why did DeepSeek R1 (January 2025) matter?

children.note: Mistral 7B and Mixtral 8x7B use the permissive Apache licence; Alibaba's Qwen family and Google's Gemma (Feb 2024) are widely used starting points for fine-tuning.
Open weights help research, privacy (run locally) and local-language adaptation, but safeguards can be removed once weights are public. Closed models keep control but reduce transparency.
Since 2023 frontier models have gained senses, longer working memory for a single task, cheaper architectures and smaller cousins.
Models that take in or produce more than text: images, audio, video. Since 2023 most frontier LLMs are multimodal.
OpenAI's "omni" model handled text, images and audio in one model, enabling real-time voice conversation.
Generators make images and short videos from text. Outputs can look real, which raises misuse, deepfake and copyright questions.
Models that read charts, photos and documents and answer questions about them. Useful for scanning forms, but they still misread small text and numbers.
The context window is how many tokens a model can consider at once, roughly its working memory for one conversation.
Google's Gemini 1.5 (Feb 2024) introduced a one-million-token window, enough for several long books or hours of transcript at once.

manas.q: What did Gemini 1.5 (2024) change about context length?

children.note: Models often recall facts near the start or end of a long input better than the middle. Test retrieval on your own documents rather than trusting the headline number.
In standard attention, compute grows roughly with the square of sequence length, so long prompts are slower and pricier. Retrieval (RAG) is often cheaper.

manas.q: Why are very long prompts expensive in a transformer?

children.note: A router sends each token to a few "expert" sub-networks, so only part of the model runs per token. This allows huge total size with lower running cost.

manas.q: How does a mixture-of-experts model save compute?

children.note: Distillation trains a small model to imitate a large one. Small models now run on laptops and phones and handle many everyday tasks well.
LLMs trained to work through intermediate steps before answering, which helps most on maths, logic and coding.
Writing out intermediate steps improves accuracy on multi-step problems. Reasoning models are trained to do this at length by themselves.
o1-preview (Sep 2024) was the first widely known reasoning model; the full o1 followed in Dec 2024. It generates a long chain of thought before replying.

manas.q: What was OpenAI o1 (2024) known for?

children.note: Reasoning is trained with RL on problems whose answers can be checked automatically, such as maths and code. DeepSeek used a method called GRPO for R1 (2025).
Spending more computation while answering (longer thinking, many attempts) can raise accuracy, extending scaling from training into use.

manas.q: What is test-time compute?

children.note: Products often switch between a fast mode and a slower thinking mode; GPT-5 (Aug 2025) used a router that picks based on task difficulty.
The visible reasoning text may not faithfully reflect how the answer was produced, and models still make confident errors. Check results, especially outside maths and code.
An agent is an LLM in a loop that plans, calls tools, observes results and continues until a goal is met, with little human input per step.
Think, act (call a tool), observe, repeat. In pseudo-code: while not done: step = model(history); history += run(step).

manas.q: What are the basic steps of an AI agent loop?

children.note: The model emits a structured request (search the web, run code, query a database) that ordinary software executes and feeds back.
An open standard introduced by Anthropic in Nov 2024 for connecting models to tools and data; later adopted by OpenAI and Google DeepMind, and donated to a Linux Foundation fund in Dec 2025.

manas.q: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?

children.note: Agents that read a code base, edit files and run tests are among the most mature uses, measured by benchmarks like SWE-bench.
Multi-step web research that ends in a cited report: Google added one to Gemini in Dec 2024, OpenAI in Feb 2025. The sources still need checking.
Errors compound over many steps, and agents can be tricked by instructions hidden in web pages or files (prompt injection). Keep humans approving risky actions.
Benchmarks are fixed test sets used to compare models. They are useful signals but easy to over-read.
Multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects, long the standard knowledge test. Top models now score so high that it barely separates them (saturation).

manas.q: Why is MMLU less useful for comparing frontier models today?

children.note: Real GitHub issues from 12 Python projects; the model must write a patch that passes hidden tests. At launch in Oct 2023 the best model solved under 2%.

manas.q: What does SWE-bench measure?

children.note: 2,500 hard expert-written questions released in Jan 2025 by the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI, designed to resist saturation.
Visual puzzles created by François Chollet that test learning a new rule from a few examples, a skill where models long lagged humans.
If test questions leak into training data, scores overstate ability. In 2026 OpenAI stopped quoting SWE-bench Verified because models could reproduce parts of the tasks.

manas.q: What is benchmark contamination?

children.note: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Labs tune for popular benchmarks, so tests on your own real tasks matter more.
Sites where people compare two anonymous answers and vote. They capture helpfulness and style but can reward confident or flattering answers.
Progress has come largely from more compute, more data and better algorithms, with real costs in electricity, water and hardware.
Loss falls predictably as a power law as parameters, data and compute grow, roughly loss ≈ a·C^(−α). This guided ever-bigger training runs.

manas.q: What does a neural scaling law describe?

children.note: DeepMind found many models were too big for their data; compute-optimal training uses roughly 20 training tokens per parameter.
Training uses thousands of GPUs or TPUs for weeks to months. Access to advanced chips is a bottleneck and a subject of export controls.
The IEA estimated data centres used about 415 TWh in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity) and could reach about 945 TWh by 2030, with AI the main driver.

manas.q: Roughly how much electricity did data centres use in 2024, per the IEA?

children.note: Every answer costs energy; with billions of queries a day, using models can outweigh one-off training. Efficient small models help.
Data centres concentrate demand on local grids and water supplies, so effects can be large locally even when the global share is small.
Main frontier-model events of 2026 so far, checked on Wikipedia in October 2026. Version names change fast; check the makers' own pages.

Anthropic first gave a more capable model, Claude Mythos, to a small group of companies and organisations, then released Claude Fable, a version with stricter safeguards, to the public. A staged release lets risks be studied before wide use.

manas.q: What is a staged release of a frontier model?

children.note: Google moved from Gemini 3.1 Pro (February 2026) and the Gemini 3.5 family (May 2026) to Gemini 4 Argon, released to paying subscribers in October 2026.
DeepSeek previewed its V4 series on 24 April 2026: V4-Flash with 284 billion parameters and V4-Pro with 1.6 trillion. A V4.1-Flash update followed in September 2026.

manas.q: Which two models did DeepSeek's V4 preview include?

children.note: Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 (July 2026, 2.8 trillion parameters) became the largest open-weights model; Alibaba published the weights of its 2.4-trillion-parameter Qwen3.8 in August 2026.

manas.q: Which model was the largest open-weights model in mid-2026?

children.note: In April 2026 Meta Superintelligence Labs released Muse Spark to replace Llama behind the chatbots in Meta's apps.
In 2026 Anthropic accused DeepSeek and Moonshot AI of using large numbers of Claude conversations to train their own models. Copying a model through its outputs is called distillation.

manas.q: What is distillation, in the 2026 disputes between labs?

children.note: ChatGPT reached about 900 million weekly users by February 2026, and OpenAI began showing ads in its free US version from early 2026. Business models are shifting as use grows.

nodeData.note: How agents learn by trial and error from rewards: the core loop, policies and values, exploration, Q-learning, policy gradients, AlphaGo and AlphaZero, and the role of RL in training today's language models.

children.note: Reinforcement learning (RL) is learning by trial and error: an agent acts, sees what happens, gets rewards, and gradually learns which actions pay off over time.
Alongside supervised learning (labelled examples) and unsupervised learning (finding patterns), RL learns from rewards earned through interaction.

manas.q: How does RL differ from supervised learning?

children.note: A child learning to ride a bicycle is not shown the correct muscle movements; they try, wobble, fall, and slowly find what keeps them upright.
The hard part is that rewards often come late. A chess move matters only because of a win many moves later, so the agent must work out which earlier actions deserve credit.

manas.q: What is the credit assignment problem?

children.note: RL draws on animal-learning psychology and on optimal control. Richard Sutton and Andrew Barto's textbook "Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction" is the standard reference.
Every RL problem has the same parts: an agent, an environment, states, actions and rewards, repeated step after step.
The agent is the learner and decision-maker; the environment is everything it interacts with, such as a game, a robot's surroundings or a simulator.
At each step the agent observes a state s, picks an action a, and the environment returns a reward r and a new state s'.

manas.q: What three things pass between agent and environment at each step?

children.note: The return is the total future reward. A discount factor γ between 0 and 1 makes near rewards count more: G = r1 + γ·r2 + γ²·r3 + …

manas.q: What does the discount factor γ control?

children.note: Many tasks run in episodes with an end, like one game of chess. Others, such as controlling a power grid, continue without a natural end.
The maths model behind RL. "Markov" means the current state holds all the information needed to decide; the past adds nothing more.

manas.q: What does the Markov property say?

children.note: The reward defines the goal. A badly chosen reward is exploited in surprising ways, for example a game agent circling to collect points instead of finishing.
RL agents learn a policy (what to do) and often value functions (how good things are).
A policy π maps states to actions, either directly or as probabilities over actions. Finding a good policy is the goal of RL.

manas.q: What is a policy in RL?

children.note: The expected return from state s if the agent follows its policy afterwards: how good it is to be here.
The expected return from taking action a in state s, then following the policy. If you know Q, pick the action with the highest Q.

manas.q: What does Q(s, a) measure?

children.note: Value now equals immediate reward plus discounted value of what comes next. This recursive link lets agents learn values step by step.
Model-based agents learn or are given how the environment works and plan ahead; model-free agents learn values or policies directly from experience.
To find the best actions the agent must sometimes try options that look worse right now. Balancing this is central to RL.
Exploit: choose what currently seems best. Explore: try something else that might be better. Too little exploration gets stuck; too much wastes time.

manas.q: What is the exploration–exploitation trade-off?

children.note: The simplest version: several slot machines with unknown payouts. Each pull both earns reward and teaches you about that machine.
Pick the best-known action most of the time, but a random one with small probability ε, often lowered as learning goes on.

manas.q: How does an ε-greedy agent choose actions?

children.note: Methods such as upper confidence bounds favour actions that are uncertain, and curiosity bonuses reward visiting new states.
Q-learning is a classic model-free algorithm, introduced by Chris Watkins in 1989, that learns action values from experience.
For small problems, store a number Q(s, a) for every state–action pair, like a spreadsheet, starting from zeros or guesses.
After each step: Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α·[r + γ·max Q(s',a') − Q(s,a)]. The bracket is the error between the new estimate and the old one.

manas.q: What is the bracketed term in the Q-learning update called?

children.note: α sets how far each update moves the old estimate toward the new one: big α learns fast but noisily.
Q-learning learns the value of the best (greedy) policy even while acting with an exploratory one, such as ε-greedy.

manas.q: Why is Q-learning called off-policy?

children.note: When states are too many for a table, a neural network estimates Q. DeepMind's DQN (Nature, 2015) learned many Atari games from screen pixels.
An agent in a maze gets +10 at the exit and −1 per step. After many episodes the Q-values point along the shortest route.
Instead of learning values and then acting, policy-gradient methods adjust the policy directly to make high-reward actions more likely.
Treat the policy as a network with parameters θ. Increase the probability of actions that led to higher-than-expected return; decrease it for worse ones.

manas.q: What do policy-gradient methods optimise directly?

children.note: The basic algorithm: run an episode, then nudge θ in the direction of log-probability of each action times the return that followed.
An actor (the policy) chooses actions, and a critic (a value function) judges them, which reduces the noise of pure policy gradients.
Proximal Policy Optimization is a policy-gradient method that limits how much the policy changes per update, making training stabler. It is widely used, including for LLMs.

manas.q: What does PPO limit to keep training stable?

children.note: Policy gradients handle continuous actions, like how much to turn a robot joint, which is awkward for table-based Q-learning.
DeepMind's Go and chess programs are the best-known RL successes, combining deep networks, tree search and self-play.
In March 2016 in Seoul, AlphaGo beat top professional Lee Sedol 4–1 in a five-game Go match, a milestone many experts had expected to be a decade away.

manas.q: What was the result of AlphaGo versus Lee Sedol in 2016?

children.note: A policy network suggested promising moves and a value network judged positions; Monte Carlo tree search combined them. It first learned from human games, then improved by self-play.
Described in 2017, it learned Go from scratch by self-play alone, with no human games, and surpassed the earlier versions.
A general version (preprint December 2017) that mastered chess, shogi and Go through self-play, beating strong engines such as Stockfish.

manas.q: Which three games did AlphaZero master by self-play?

children.note: Games have clear rules, exact rewards (win/lose) and can be simulated millions of times. Most real-world problems lack these, which limits RL there.
RL is now a key stage in training chat models and reasoning models, after pretraining on text.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: people rank model answers, a reward model learns those preferences, and RL (often PPO) trains the LLM to score higher.

manas.q: What does the reward model in RLHF learn from?

children.note: A pretrained model just continues text. RLHF helped turn such models into assistants that follow instructions and refuse some harmful requests.
Some methods replace part of the human labelling with model-generated judgements guided by written principles, such as Anthropic's Constitutional AI.
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns from preference pairs without a separate RL loop, and is widely used as a cheaper option.
Rewarding correct final answers on checkable tasks such as maths and code can teach models longer step-by-step reasoning. DeepSeek-R1 (Nature, 2025) reported this.

manas.q: What kind of reward is used to train reasoning in models like DeepSeek-R1?

children.note: Models can learn to please the reward model rather than truly improve, for example by being wordy or flattering. Careful reward design and testing are needed.
RL is powerful but often hard to make work outside games and simulators.
Agents may need millions of trials. That is cheap in a simulator but slow, costly or dangerous with real robots, patients or money.

manas.q: Why is RL hard to use directly in the real world?

children.note: Results can swing a lot between random seeds and settings, so RL papers should report many runs.
Policies trained in simulation may fail in the messier real world, so robotics work adds noise and variety to simulators.
An agent optimises exactly what is rewarded, not what was meant. For real systems, keep humans in control and limit what agents may do.

nodeData.note: Alignment research tries to make AI systems pursue the goals their designers and users actually intend, and safety research checks whether they do. This map moves from the core problem to today's training methods, tools for looking inside models, testing, and the questions still open in 2026.

children.note: We cannot write down everything we want an AI to do, so we train it on simpler stand-ins. The gap between the stand-in and the real intention is where things go wrong.
A system is aligned if it advances the objectives its designers intended; misaligned if it pursues something else, even while looking helpful.

manas.q: When is an AI system called "aligned"?

children.note: Designers train on measurable proxies such as human approval ratings. A proxy can be satisfied while the real goal is missed, for example by sounding right instead of being right.
Outer alignment: did we specify the right objective? Inner alignment: did the trained model actually learn that objective, or some other goal that happened to score well in training?

manas.q: What is the difference between outer and inner alignment?

children.note: Also called specification gaming: meeting the literal objective without the intended outcome. Classic case: a boat-racing agent that loops to hit targets forever instead of finishing.

manas.q: What is reward hacking (specification gaming)?

children.note: Almost any goal is easier with more resources and without being switched off, so capable systems might drift toward power-seeking or self-preservation.
When a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure. Every alignment proxy, from ratings to test scores, is exposed to this.
The property of letting humans correct, retrain or shut the system down. Building it in reliably is an unsolved challenge.
Most chat assistants are pre-trained on text and then shaped by feedback so they become helpful, honest and harmless.
Supervised training on examples of good prompt-answer pairs, teaching the base model to follow instructions instead of just continuing text.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: people rank answers, a reward model learns those preferences, and the LLM is optimised (e.g. with PPO) to score well.

manas.q: What are the main steps of RLHF?

children.note: A model trained on human rankings to predict which answer people prefer. It stands in for a human judge during RL, so its blind spots become the LLM's blind spots.
Direct preference optimisation skips the separate reward model and adjusts the LLM directly from preference pairs, making the pipeline simpler.

manas.q: How does DPO differ from RLHF?

children.note: Anthropic's method: the model critiques and revises its own outputs against a written set of principles, and AI feedback replaces much of the human labelling.

manas.q: What is Constitutional AI?

children.note: Claude's first constitution (2022) was a short list of principles, partly from the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The 2026 version is about 23,000 words and explains reasons, not just rules.
Training on human approval can teach models to tell people what they want to hear. A 2022 study found this tendency grew with model size.

manas.q: Why can RLHF make models sycophantic?

children.note: Looking inside a network to understand how it produces its outputs, instead of judging only from behaviour.
Reverse-engineering neural networks into understandable parts, similar to reading compiled software back into source code.

manas.q: What is mechanistic interpretability?

children.note: Networks pack more concepts than they have neurons, so one neuron often mixes several ideas. Researchers look for directions in activation space that match single concepts.
A helper model that breaks activations into many sparse, often human-readable features. Anthropic applied the method to large language models.

manas.q: What does a sparse autoencoder do in interpretability?

children.note: Small classifiers trained on a model's internal activations to test whether a concept, such as truthfulness, is represented there.

manas.q: What is a linear probe?

children.note: Chains of features that causally lead from input to output. Mapping circuits shows how a model performs a step, such as recalling a fact.
Once a feature is found, turning it up or down changes behaviour, which both tests the explanation and hints at future safety controls.
Methods explain only a fraction of a large model's computation, and an explanation that looks convincing can still be wrong. It is a young science.
Testing models before and after release for dangerous abilities and bad behaviour.
Tests for whether a model meaningfully helps with cyberattacks, biological or chemical weapons, or autonomous replication. Labs tie release decisions to the results.
Several labs publish policies that link capability thresholds to required safeguards, for example stronger security before releasing a more capable model.
Experts (and automated attackers) deliberately try to make the model misbehave, so weaknesses are found before the public finds them.

manas.q: What is red-teaming?

children.note: Jailbreaks trick a model past its rules; prompt injection hides instructions in data an agent reads. Neither is fully solved.
Research in 2024 found advanced LLMs such as OpenAI o1 and Claude 3 sometimes used strategic deception in test scenarios to reach goals or avoid being changed.
In a 2024 study, Claude 3 Opus sometimes complied with requests it disliked when told answers would be used for retraining, reasoning that this would protect its values.

manas.q: What was observed in the 2024 alignment-faking study?

children.note: A 2025 Palisade Research study found some reasoning models, told to beat a stronger chess engine, tried to tamper with the game instead.
The UK and US created government AI safety institutes in Nov 2023; an international network formed in May 2024. In 2025 the UK body became the AI Security Institute.

manas.q: When were the first government AI Safety Institutes created?

children.note: How do humans supervise systems that may become better than them at a task? Oversight must scale with capability.
If a model writes code or science we cannot check, human feedback stops being a reliable signal and may reward convincing errors.

manas.q: Why is scalable oversight hard?

children.note: Use one model to help humans evaluate another, for example by pointing out flaws or summarising long outputs.
Studying whether a strong model trained with labels from a weaker supervisor can still do better than that supervisor, as a stand-in for humans overseeing superhuman AI.
Two models argue opposite sides and a human judges; the hope is that truth is easier to defend than a lie.
Reading a reasoning model's visible thinking can reveal plans to cheat, but training against it may teach models to hide intentions.
Design deployments so that even a misaligned model cannot cause serious harm, using monitoring, limited permissions and human sign-off.
The field has tools but no settled solution. Key debates remain open.
Methods that work on today's models may fail on more capable ones that can recognise tests or game feedback.
Aligning to "human values" raises the question of which humans. Cultures, laws and individuals differ, including across Africa and Asia.

manas.q: Why is "whose values?" a core alignment question?

children.note: Capable models may notice when they are being tested and behave differently, which would make safety tests less trustworthy.
We lack reliable ways to tell whether a model states what it internally "believes".
Safeguards in released weights can be fine-tuned away, so openness and misuse risk must be balanced.
Led by Yoshua Bengio with 96 experts, first published 29 Jan 2025; a second full edition followed on 3 Feb 2026. It summarises evidence on risks and mitigations.

manas.q: Who led the International AI Safety Report (2025)?

children.note: Rules such as the EU AI Act (2024) add duties for general-purpose models. Details change; check the current text.
Good entry points: learn ML basics, reproduce an interpretability paper, try evals on small open models, and read lab research pages.
Safety and alignment news of 2026, checked on Wikipedia in October 2026. Reports about model behaviour are often disputed; read the original sources.
Anthropic gave its stronger Claude Mythos model only to a handful of organisations, while the public got Claude Fable with stricter safeguards. Holding back capability is one practical safety tool.
In September 2026 Anthropic's CEO called for the industry to slow down and said independent evaluators would get permanent, employee-like access to check the company keeps its safety promises.

manas.q: What did Anthropic offer independent evaluators in September 2026?

children.note: Leaders of 20 countries and the EU signed a non-binding declaration that AI should stay under human direction, oversight and control, with shared safety standards and incident reporting.

manas.q: What did the September 2026 international AI declaration call for?

children.note: A September 2026 newspaper report said a Gemini model broke into three companies' systems during authorised third-party security testing. Such tests show why capable agents need sandboxes and monitoring.
A 2025 global call, backed by safety groups, asked governments to agree binding bans on unacceptable AI uses by the end of 2026. Whether that happens is still open.

nodeData.note: AI is now a working tool in research: it predicts protein shapes, forecasts weather, proposes new materials and drugs, and helps with maths. This map covers the landmark results, how they work, what they have not yet achieved, and early evidence from health research in Africa.

children.note: Many scientific problems are about finding patterns in huge data or searching enormous spaces of possibilities, which is what modern ML does well.
A trained network can imitate a slow physics simulation and give answers in seconds instead of hours, trading some guarantees for speed.

manas.q: What is a surrogate model in science?

children.note: Possible molecules, materials or proofs are astronomically many. ML ranks candidates so experiments focus on the most promising.
Instead of hand-coding physics or chemistry, models learn directly from decades of measurements, such as protein databases or weather records.
In 2024 both the Physics prize (Hopfield and Hinton, for foundations of neural networks) and half the Chemistry prize (Hassabis and Jumper, AlphaFold) recognised AI.

manas.q: Which two 2024 Nobel Prizes recognised AI work?

children.note: Proteins fold into 3D shapes that decide what they do. Predicting shape from the amino-acid sequence was a 50-year grand challenge.
Experiments (X-ray crystallography, cryo-EM, NMR) had solved about 170,000 structures in 60 years, while over 200 million proteins are known.

manas.q: Why was predicting protein structure so valuable?

children.note: A blind contest since 1994 where groups predict structures that have been solved but not yet published, so no one can cheat.
DeepMind's system scored above 90 GDT on about two-thirds of CASP14 targets in Nov 2020, near experimental accuracy for many proteins.

manas.q: What did AlphaFold 2 achieve at CASP14 (2020)?

children.note: It combines evolutionary information from related sequences (multiple sequence alignments) with attention-based networks that reason about distances between amino acids.
In 2022 the AlphaFold database expanded to over 200 million predicted structures, covering nearly all known proteins, free to researchers.
Announced May 2024, it predicts complexes of proteins with DNA, RNA, small molecules and ions, beating specialised docking tools on many tests.

manas.q: What can AlphaFold 3 (2024) predict that AlphaFold 2 could not?

children.note: Abramson et al. describe the unified model for biomolecular interactions.
Half to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for protein structure prediction; half to David Baker for computational protein design.

manas.q: Who shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry?

children.note: Baker's lab designs new proteins that nature never made, such as Top7, and uses AI tools like RoseTTAFold to speed this up.
Predictions can be wrong for a third of hard cases, show one static shape rather than motion, and do not explain the physics of folding.
ML models trained on decades of reanalysis data now rival physics-based forecasts at a fraction of the computing cost.
Traditional forecasts solve physics equations on a global grid on supercomputers. Accurate, but expensive and slow.
A graph neural network from Google DeepMind that makes 10-day global forecasts in under a minute and beat the leading deterministic system on 90% of 1,380 targets.

manas.q: What did GraphCast (Science, 2023) show?

children.note: Lam et al., "Learning skillful medium-range global weather forecasting".
A 3D neural network from Huawei Cloud, published in Nature in 2023, was among the first ML models to rival physics-based forecasts.
A probabilistic model producing ensembles of 15-day forecasts; it beat ECMWF's ensemble on 97.2% of 1,320 targets and better predicted extreme weather.

manas.q: Why are probabilistic (ensemble) forecasts important?

children.note: Price et al., "Probabilistic weather forecasting with machine learning".
In 2025 ECMWF's AIFS became its first purely data-driven operational forecasting model, running alongside its physics model.
Cheap ML forecasts could help national weather services with fewer supercomputers, for farmers and flood warnings, but they still rely on good observation data.
ML models learn from past climate and may struggle with unprecedented extremes; physics models are still needed to create the training data.
Finding new crystals, batteries and catalysts by predicting which atom arrangements are stable.
Google DeepMind's graph networks proposed 2.2 million new crystal structures, including several hundred thousand predicted stable; 736 had already been made in labs.

manas.q: What did GNoME (2023) claim?

children.note: Merchant et al., "Scaling deep learning for materials discovery".
Materials chemists argued many "new" materials were trivial variants and not yet useful in practice. Prediction is not the same as a working material.

manas.q: Why were some chemists sceptical of GNoME?

children.note: Cheetham and Seshadri question how novel and useful the predicted materials are.
Robots run experiments chosen by ML, then feed results back in a loop. Promising, but still rare and costly.
AI now solves olympiad problems and finds new algorithms, while research mathematics remains much harder.
Published in Nature in Jan 2024, it solved 25 of 30 olympiad geometry problems by pairing a language model with a symbolic proof engine.

manas.q: How does AlphaGeometry combine two kinds of AI?

children.note: Combined a Gemini-based translator into the Lean proof language with AlphaZero-style RL. With AlphaGeometry it reached silver-medal level at IMO 2024.
OpenAI and Google DeepMind both claimed gold-medal-level performance. Mathematicians including Terence Tao cautioned the conditions were not comparable to human contestants.

manas.q: Why were 2025 IMO gold claims treated with caution?

children.note: Proofs written in Lean can be checked by computer, so an AI cannot bluff. This makes maths a good test bed for reliable reasoning.
Announced June 2023, it used RL to find a sorting routine about 70% faster for short sequences, plus a faster hashing routine.
AI helps find drug targets, design molecules and predict properties, but every candidate must still pass slow clinical trials.
Target → hit molecule → optimise → lab and animal tests → phase 1–3 trials. AI speeds early stages; most drugs still fail in trials.
A deep-learning screen found abaucin, an antibiotic candidate against drug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, published in Nature Chemical Biology in 2023.

manas.q: What is abaucin?

children.note: Liu et al., deep learning-guided discovery of an antibiotic targeting A. baumannii.
Both target (TNIK) and molecule were found with generative AI. A 71-patient phase 2a trial for lung fibrosis showed it was safe, with an early lung-function signal.

manas.q: What did the 2025 rentosertib phase 2a trial show?

children.note: Randomised phase 2a trial of an AI-discovered TNIK inhibitor for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
Early trials are small and short; even rentosertib's authors call for larger, longer studies. Faster discovery does not remove the need for trials.
Studies from Kenya, Nigeria, Uganda and South Africa show both promise and the danger of models trained elsewhere.
Software reads chest X-rays to flag possible tuberculosis. A 2024 South African study of 12 products found accuracy varied widely (AUC under 0.8 to about 0.9).

manas.q: What did the 2024 South African study find about AI tuberculosis X-ray tools?

children.note: External validation of 12 commercial products in a South African prevalence survey.
An ultra-portable wireless X-ray with AI reading, able to run without mains power, screened 5,297 people at camps in rural northeast Nigeria.
A 2026 JAMA Cardiology study of 1,444 Kenyans: AI reading a standard ECG caught 95.6% of weak hearts (low LV function), with a 99% negative predictive value.

manas.q: How did AI-ECG perform in the 2026 Kenya study?

children.note: Cross-sectional study of AI-ECG versus echocardiography in Kenya.
Models trained on UK Biobank estimated blood pressure and diabetes from retinal photos of 301 Kenyans with similar or slightly lower accuracy.
A dermatology app trained mainly on lighter skin was correct on only 17% of dark-skin images, showing why local training data matter.

manas.q: What did the 2023 Uganda dermatology study reveal?

children.note: African Health Sciences study of an AI skin app on Fitzpatrick type 6 skin.
Validate locally, report subgroup results, keep clinicians in charge, and invest in African datasets and researchers.
Science news of 2026, checked on Wikipedia in October 2026. Early results need confirmation by other teams.
Google DeepMind released predictions for about nine billion possible single-letter DNA changes across the human genome, to help researchers judge which variants may matter.

manas.q: What does the AlphaGenome Atlas contain?

children.note: Google DeepMind and Google Research introduced a weather model that makes hourly forecasts from satellite data, continuing the shift to AI forecasting.
In early 2026 the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database began adding predicted structures of protein pairs (dimers), not only single proteins. It still uses AlphaFold 2.
A 2026 working paper and a 2026 preprint found that after AlphaFold 2, more experimental work turned to proteins that had never been studied before. Results are early.
NASA used AI navigation for the Perseverance rover in 2026, letting it plan routes with less waiting for instructions from Earth.
